title: Superconductivity in Noncentrosymmetric NbReSi: Beyond Harmonic and Adiabatic Limits
authors: Shashi B. Mishra, Sohair ElMeligy, Pratibha Dev
abstract: The noncentrosymmetric superconductor NbReSi (Tc=6.5 K) is being actively explored for unconventional pairing that is allowed by its broken inversion symmetry. Despite broad experimental interest, what drives its superconductivity remains an open question. We show that the electronic states at the Fermi level are dominated by Nb and Re $d$-states. Vibrations of the same heavy-metal framework contribute more than 95% of the electron-phonon coupling, with the strongest coupling arising from the sublattice-selective breathing mode involving strongly bonded Re atoms. Harmonic Migdal-Eliashberg theory overestimates Tc by more than 60%. The zero-point anharmonic hardening of these modes reduces the coupling by 20%. The leading vertex correction becomes important as well despite low phonon energies due to the contribution of spatially localized Re-d orbitals to the electronic band structure near the Fermi level. Together, anharmonicity and vertex corrections bring the calculated Tc and superconducting gap into close agreement with experiment, establishing NbReSi as a moderately coupled, phonon-mediated superconductor whose quantitative description requires going beyond harmonic Migdal--Eliashberg theory.
summary: This work investigates superconductivity in NbReSi, finding that while the pairing is phonon-mediated, standard theoretical models overestimate the critical temperature. The authors successfully reconcile theory with experiment by rigorously including anharmonic lattice effects and electron-phonon vertex corrections, establishing a quantitative understanding of the pairing mechanism.
main_problem: To determine the microscopic origin of superconductivity in the noncentrosymmetric material NbReSi and to accurately calculate its critical temperature ($T_c$).
main_result: The superconductivity is established as phonon-mediated, but quantitative agreement with experiment requires going beyond harmonic Migdal-Eliashberg theory by including anharmonic lattice dynamics and vertex corrections.
method: The study uses first-principles calculations (DFT/DFPT) to solve the isotropic Eliashberg equations, incorporating anharmonic phonon renormalization and lowest-order electron-phonon vertex corrections.
model_or_system: The system is the noncentrosymmetric superconductor NbReSi. The theory models electron-phonon coupling ($\lambda$) and the superconducting gap ($\Delta$) using advanced many-body techniques.
key_observables: Superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$), superconducting gap ($\Delta(0)$), electron-phonon coupling constant ($\lambda$), and phonon frequencies ($\omega$).
important_parameters: The necessity of anharmonicity and vertex corrections to match the experimental $T_c$ of 6.5 K.
main_assumptions: The initial assumption of conventional phonon-mediated pairing is tested against advanced theoretical limits (harmonic vs. anharmonic, with/without vertex corrections).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate electronic structure, phonon dispersion (comparing harmonic and anharmonic treatments), and the Eliashberg spectral function $\alpha^2F(\omega)$ under various theoretical approximations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the electronic structure, then calculating the electron-phonon coupling using harmonic theory, demonstrating its overestimation of $T_c$, and finally refining the calculation by incorporating anharmonicity and vertex corrections to match experimental results.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state physics, the rigorous application of advanced many-body perturbation theory (Eliashberg equations) to model emergent quantum phenomena like superconductivity is relevant to understanding strongly coupled quantum systems.

Figure 1(a) compares the electronic bands without and with SOC. The largest SOC splittings, about 0.2 eV at Γ- and A-points, agree with the earlier report [2]. These splittings arise in the bands that are mostly derived from the d-orbitals of the heavy elements – Nb and Re. The Kramers’ degeneracy is preserved at Γ and A since these are time-reversal-invariant-momenta points. The bands crossing εF split by less than 25 meV, so ASOC leaves the Fermi-level electronic structure essentially unchanged and modifies the electron-phonon coupling by only 4% (Fig. S4 [25]), indicating its minor role in superconduct- ing pairing, if any.
